title: Study Strategies and Exam Preparation
summary: Active study methods, spaced practice and self-testing, a revision timetable, understanding question verbs and mark allocations, exam-room strategies and learning from results.

notes.text: **Passive** studying (only re-reading or highlighting) feels easy but is not very effective. **Active** studying makes your brain work to recall and use information, so you remember much more.

rows: Close your book and write or say everything you remember; then check what you missed
Revise a topic several times over days and weeks, rather than once in a long session
Mix different types of problems in one session (e.g. different kinds of Maths questions)
Ask yourself 'why?' and 'how?' and connect new ideas to what you already know
Condense notes into key points and diagrams in your own words
Practise under timed exam conditions and mark your work with the memo

items: Start at least **four weeks** before exams.
List all subjects and topics; spend more time on difficult topics.
Plan **specific tasks** (e.g. 'Science: do 10 questions on acids') rather than vague goals ('study Science').
Include breaks, exercise, meals and 8 or more hours of sleep.
Review your plan weekly and adjust it.

rows: Give the exact meaning of a term
Give the characteristics or details of something
Give reasons or show how or why something happens
Examine different points of view or aspects, with evidence
Judge the value or success of something and give reasons

notes.label: Exam tip
notes.text: Use the **mark allocation** as a guide: a 3-mark 'explain' question usually needs three clear points or a point with explanation and an example.

items: Read the instructions and the whole paper first (use the reading time).
Plan your time: roughly one minute per mark.
Answer the questions you know well first, but number answers correctly.
Underline key words in each question.
Write clearly and in full sentences where needed.
Leave time to check your answers.

notes.text: When you get your results, look at your mistakes and work out **why** you lost marks: lack of knowledge, misreading the question, poor time management or careless errors. Use this to improve your study plan. A disappointing result is information, not failure.

questions.prompt: Give THREE tips for an effective revision timetable.
questions.memo: Any three (1 each): start early; more time for difficult topics; specific tasks; include breaks and sleep; review weekly; realistic

questions.prompt: Why is re-reading notes less effective than self-testing?
questions.memo:
✓ Re-reading is passive; it feels familiar but does not make you recall (1)
✓ Self-testing makes the brain retrieve information, which strengthens memory (1)

questions.prompt: Describe THREE strategies to use in the exam room.
questions.memo: Any three (1 each): read instructions/whole paper; plan time; answer known questions first; underline key words; number correctly; check answers

questions.prompt: How can a learner use exam results to improve?
questions.memo:
✓ Analyse mistakes to find why marks were lost (1)
✓ Adjust the study plan / practise weak areas (1)

questions.prompt: How does the mark allocation help you answer a question?
questions.memo:
✓ It shows how many points or how much detail is expected (1)
✓ It helps you plan time and avoid writing too much or too little (1)
